subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Ectopic Pregnancy: Sites, Rupture and Haemoperitoneum

steps.tx: Implantation of pregnancy outside the uterine cavity is an **ectopic pregnancy**. Over ninety five percent occur in the fallopian tube, most often its ampullary part. It complicates one to two percent of pregnancies and remains a leading early maternal killer. Prior chlamydia infection is the single biggest driver of the tubal damage behind most cases.
steps.say: Ectopic pregnancy implants outside the cavity, mostly in the tubal ampulla.

steps.tx: The widest tubal segment where most ectopics implant and may abort through the fimbriae is the **ampulla**. Ampullary pregnancies often present as tubal abortion rather than rupture. Blood trickles into the peritoneum causing gradual symptoms. Tubal abortion often settles briefly, then rebleeds, giving a stuttering course over days rather than minutes.
steps.say: The ampulla hosts most ectopics, which often abort through the fimbriae gradually.

steps.tx: The narrow tubal segment rupturing earliest, around six weeks, is the **isthmus**. It cannot distend, so even small pregnancies split it. Presentation is correspondingly earlier and more acute than ampullary disease. Pain often starts by six to eight weeks, earlier than the classic eight to ten weeks of ampullary rupture.
steps.say: The isthmus ruptures earliest because it cannot distend around the pregnancy.

steps.tx: The tubal segment that ruptures earliest, around six weeks, is the **isthmus**. It cannot stretch, so a small pregnancy splits it, and pain often starts by six to eight weeks rather than the eight to ten weeks typical of ampullary rupture. Blood then pours into the peritoneal cavity, settles in the pouch of Douglas, and produces haemoperitoneum. Ampullary pregnancies have more room to expand before they tear, which is why their collapse tends to come later.
steps.say: The isthmus is too narrow to distend, so a tubal pregnancy there ruptures around six weeks, with pain often by six to eight weeks. Ampullary rupture more often waits until eight to ten weeks. Once the tube splits, blood fills the peritoneal cavity and pools in the pouch of Douglas.

vis.alt: A ruptured tubal ectopic pregnancy spilling blood into the peritoneal cavity and the pouch of Douglas.
vis.caption: A split fallopian tube bleeds into the pelvis, and blood collects in the pouch of Douglas. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Splitting of the tube with bleeding into the abdomen is **tubal rupture**. Sudden severe pain, shoulder tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation and fainting follow. The clinical triad of amenorrhoea, pain and bleeding may be incomplete, so suspicion must stay high. Blood under the diaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve, C3 to C5, which is why shoulder tip pain appears.
steps.say: Tubal rupture causes sudden pain, shoulder tip pain and fainting from internal bleeding.

steps.tx: Free blood in the peritoneal cavity from rupture is **haemoperitoneum**. It produces peritonism, tachycardia and falling haemoglobin. Resuscitation with blood and immediate surgery are simultaneous priorities in the unstable patient. A falling haemoglobin with a rigid abdomen and a positive test in a shocked woman means theatre, not more scans.
steps.say: Haemoperitoneum from rupture needs simultaneous resuscitation, blood and surgery.

steps.tx: Risk factors damage tubal transport and include previous pelvic infection, tubal surgery and assisted conception, grouped as **tubal risk factors**. Previous ectopic pregnancy carries the highest recurrence risk. Many ectopics, however, occur with no risk factor at all. A previous ectopic raises recurrence to about one in ten, the highest single risk figure to quote.
steps.say: Tubal risk factors damage transport, though many ectopics occur with none at all.

steps.tx: Dangerous implantation in the uterine muscle segment of tube is **interstitial pregnancy**. It ruptures late, around twelve weeks, into rich uterine vessels. Haemorrhage is catastrophic and may need hysterectomy. It can grow to 12 to 16 weeks because the uterine wall stretches, which is why its rupture bleeds so heavily.
steps.say: Interstitial pregnancy ruptures late into rich vessels with catastrophic haemorrhage.

steps.tx: Free fluid in the abdomen of a shocked pregnant woman is a surgical sign. A **positive FAST equivalent** scan in suspected ectopic pregnancy means blood around the liver or in the pelvis, moving management straight to resuscitation and theatre. It answers the only question that matters at that moment: is she bleeding inside. Chasing a perfect tubal picture while the abdomen fills is the classic diagnostic delay this scan exists to prevent.
steps.say: Free intraperitoneal fluid on scan in a collapsed woman with suspected ectopic means internal bleeding. It sends management to resuscitation and theatre.

vis.alt: Ultrasound image showing free fluid in the abdomen on a FAST style scan in ectopic pregnancy.
vis.caption: Free fluid is shown around the liver on an emergency abdominal ultrasound scan. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Bedside free fluid on ultrasound with an empty uterus drives emergency action, termed **positive FAST equivalent** in pregnancy terms. In a shocked woman with positive pregnancy test, this means theatre without delay for further imaging. Bedside clotting and crossmatch run alongside, with O negative blood given when delay would be dangerous.
steps.say: Free fluid with empty uterus in a shocked pregnant woman means theatre without delay.

steps.tx: Chronic ectopic with organised pelvic blood collection forms a **pelvic haematocele**. Repeated small leaks wall off behind the uterus causing chronic pain and a tender mass. Surgery evacuates clot and removes the affected tube. It presents weeks later with a tender fixed mass behind the uterus and low grade fever, mimicking pelvic infection.
steps.say: Chronic ectopic walls off blood as a pelvic haematocele causing chronic pain.
